question: What causes most cases of sudden food-borne illness?

options.A: Direct skin contact with infected persons
options.B: Ingestion of contaminated food or water

explanation: Food-borne illnesses are transmitted primarily through eating or drinking contaminated substances. [learn more](GNS227_U3_T010#GNS227_U3_T010_h1)

question: Why do nurses ask patients about what they ate in the last 72 hours?

options.A: It helps identify the specific meal or contaminant responsible for symptoms
options.B: It confirms whether the patient has chronic hypertension
options.C: It determines the exact financial cost of the patient's groceries
options.D: It measures the patient's daily caloric intake requirements

explanation: Most food-borne pathogens have incubation periods that fall within a 24 to 72-hour window. [learn more](GNS227_U3_T010#GNS227_U3_T010_h1)

question: Which bacteria grows in poorly stored food and causes quick vomiting via preformed toxins?
explanation: Staphylococcus aureus multiplies in food and releases toxins that cause quick symptom onset without requiring active infection in the gut. [learn more](GNS227_U3_T010#GNS227_U3_T010_h2)

question: How do germs like Salmonella cause damage in the digestive tract?

options.A: By permanently neutralizing all pancreatic digestive enzymes
options.B: By dissolving the outer muscular layer of the stomach
options.C: By invading the intestinal mucosa and triggering inflammation
options.D: By completely blocking the absorption of dietary proteins

explanation: Invasive organisms penetrate the gut lining, provoking an immune response that results in mucosal injury and diarrhea. [learn more](GNS227_U3_T010#GNS227_U3_T010_h2)

question: What is the main difference between food poisoning (intoxication) and a food infection?

options.A: Infections are strictly caused by chemical cleaning agents
options.B: Intoxications are caused by ingesting preformed toxins rather than live multiplying pathogens
options.C: Intoxications always require a minimum incubation period of two weeks
options.D: Infections never involve diarrhea or abdominal cramping

explanation: Intoxications rely on poisons already present in the food prior to consumption, leading to very rapid onset. [learn more](GNS227_U3_T010#GNS227_U3_T010_h3)

question: Why do food-borne infections take longer to show symptoms than intoxications?

options.A: The ingested microorganisms must multiply inside the host before causing symptoms
options.B: Infections only spread through the respiratory bloodstream
options.C: Pathogens require time to travel to the central nervous system first
options.D: The human stomach instantly destroys all infectious microbes within seconds

explanation: Live pathogens need time to adapt, colonize, and grow in the gastrointestinal tract before clinical signs appear. [learn more](GNS227_U3_T010#GNS227_U3_T010_h3)

question: Why are infants at higher risk for severe complications from food poisoning?

options.A: They possess high levels of gastric acid protection
options.B: Their diets consist entirely of sterile mineral water
options.C: They naturally produce adequate antibodies against all toxins
options.D: They have immature immune systems and small body mass

explanation: Small body size combined with developing immunity means fluid loss and systemic infections escalate quickly in babies. [learn more](GNS227_U3_T010#GNS227_U3_T010_h4)

question: How do age-related changes in older adults increase their risk of food-borne illness?

options.A: Enhanced mucosal lining thickness blocks normal nutrient uptake
options.B: Increased liver size accelerates the clearance of beneficial bacteria
options.C: Decreased gastric acid production allows more pathogens to survive stomach transit
options.D: Higher metabolic rates cause faster toxin absorption in the colon

explanation: Stomach acid acts as a primary chemical barrier; reduced acid allows live microbes to pass unhindered into the intestines. [learn more](GNS227_U3_T010#GNS227_U3_T010_h4)

question: Which sign points to dehydration in a patient with severe vomiting and diarrhea?

options.A: Poor skin turgor and dry mucous membranes
options.D: Bounding peripheral pulses and flushed skin

explanation: Fluid loss reduces interstitial volume, resulting in dry tissues and delayed skin recoil after pinching. [learn more](GNS227_U3_T010#GNS227_U3_T010_h5)

question: When should a nurse expect a doctor to order a blood culture for food poisoning?

options.A: To measure baseline dietary caloric intake
options.B: When systemic bacteremia or sepsis is suspected
options.C: To replace routine stool sample analysis

explanation: Blood cultures help detect invasive pathogens that have crossed from the gut into the bloodstream. [learn more](GNS227_U3_T010#GNS227_U3_T010_h5)

question: What is the first-line treatment for mild to moderate dehydration from food poisoning?
explanation: Oral rehydration is safe, effective, and physiologically balanced to replace lost water and electrolytes through the gut. [learn more](GNS227_U3_T010#GNS227_U3_T010_h6)

question: Why are anti-diarrhea drugs often avoided during bacterial food poisoning?

options.A: They instantly cause permanent kidney failure in all patients
options.B: They neutralize the effectiveness of oral rehydration solutions
options.C: They trigger immediate respiratory arrest in adults
options.D: They trap pathogens and toxins inside the gut by slowing peristalsis

explanation: Slowing down bowel movements prevents the body from naturally expelling harmful bacteria and toxins. [learn more](GNS227_U3_T010#GNS227_U3_T010_h6)

question: What serious condition is linked as a complication of severe E. coli infections?

options.A: Spontaneous bone fractures in the lower extremities
options.B: Chronic inflammation of the upper respiratory airways
options.C: Acute kidney injury with hemolytic anemia and thrombocytopenia
options.D: Permanent loss of hearing and bilateral tinnitus

explanation: HUS damages small blood vessels, leading to red blood cell destruction, low platelets, and kidney failure. [learn more](GNS227_U3_T010#GNS227_U3_T010_h7)

question: How can unmanaged dehydration lead to multi-organ failure?

options.A: Fluid overload causes immediate rupture of the cerebral ventricles
options.B: Pathogens consume all circulating white blood cells within hours
options.C: Decreased blood volume leads to poor tissue perfusion and oxygen delivery
options.D: Excess salt accumulation directly dissolves the cellular walls of the heart

explanation: Extreme fluid loss drops cardiac output, starving vital organs of oxygen and nutrients. [learn more](GNS227_U3_T010#GNS227_U3_T010_h7)

question: Why is it important to separate raw meat from cooked food during meal preparation?

options.A: To improve the overall visual presentation of meals
options.B: To reduce the financial cost of kitchen utensils
options.D: To accelerate the cooking time of vegetables

explanation: Separation stops bacteria from transferring from raw animal products onto ready-to-eat foods. [learn more](GNS227_U3_T010#GNS227_U3_T010_h8)

question: How do unstable electricity supplies in places like Nigeria increase food safety risks?

options.A: Lack of electricity forces citizens to consume only raw imported grains
options.B: Power failures cause municipal water pipes to reverse water flow
options.C: Frequent power outages disrupt proper cold storage and refrigeration of perishables
options.D: Electrical fluctuations instantly destroy all vitamins present in fresh fruit

explanation: Without reliable refrigeration, bacterial growth in perishable foods accelerates rapidly at ambient room temperatures. [learn more](GNS227_U3_T010#GNS227_U3_T010_h8)
